keyVerseText: Thy servant will go a little way over Jordan with the king: and why should the king recompense it me with such a reward?
rootMeaning: The root of גְּמוּלָה (gᵉmûwlâh) is גְּמוּל (gᵉmûwl), which conveys the idea of a deed or act of service that involves recompense or reward. This root emphasizes a relational exchange—what has been given or deserved as a result of one's actions. Beyond the simple English gloss of 'reward' or 'recompense,' the root sense includes the notion of treatment or dealing, whether good or ill, highlighting the active response to behavior or service.
usageInScripture: The word גְּמוּלָה appears three times in Scripture and is consistently associated with the concept of recompense or dealing. Its translations range from 'such a reward' to 'their deeds' and 'of recompences,' showing a focus on the outcome or response to actions. This consistency underscores the word's emphasis on the tangible consequences or returns that follow from one's conduct, whether in human relationships or divine justice.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גְּמוּלָה enriches our grasp of divine justice and human responsibility in Scripture. It reminds believers that God is a God of recompense, who deals with humanity according to their deeds, rewarding faithfulness and addressing wrongdoing. This concept encourages a faith that is active and responsive, knowing that God’s dealings are just and purposeful. It also points to the grace inherent in God’s rewards, as He is the ultimate source of all recompense, which in Christ is extended beyond mere merit to mercy and salvation.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 19:36, the servant questions why the king would 'recompense it me with such a reward,' using גְּמוּלָה to express concern over the nature of the return he is receiving for his service. This word highlights the personal and relational aspect of recompense, emphasizing the servant’s expectation of a just and fitting response. It draws attention to the seriousness with which rewards and consequences are regarded in the biblical worldview, reminding us that our actions invite corresponding dealings.
